How Much Recalibration Is Enough? Reliability of Cellular Throughput Forecasts Across Networks with Missing Radio Telemetry

Md. Moazzem Hossain Majumder, Student Member, IEEE
Independent Researcher in Telecommunications and Applied Machine Learning
Email: moazzemhossain1510@gmail.com
Abstract—
Downlink throughput forecasting in modern cellular networks is critical for proactive transport-layer bandwidth provisioning, adaptive bitrate streaming, and service level agreement (SLA) assurance in fourth-generation (4G) Long Term Evolution (LTE) and fifth-generation (5G) Non-Standalone (NSA) architectures. However, supervised machine learning predictors trained in one network environment exhibit catastrophic failure when transferred across operators or measurement campaigns. This vulnerability is compounded by structural telemetry missingness, where secondary 5G New Radio (NR) synchronization indicators are absent in 63.4% of operational sessions due to discontinuous carrier aggregation and 3GPP Option 3X EN-DC state transitions. While conventional models optimize symmetric point errors, production networks require conservative, calibrated lower bounds to prevent Quality-of-Service (QoS) breaches. In this paper, we formulate an experimental benchmark addressing the fundamental question: How much target-network calibration data is required to recover dependable throughput lower bounds under natural telemetry missingness and network distribution shift? Utilizing 1,132 verified commercial Speedtest sessions across 2021 and 2023 commercial campaigns in Rome, Italy, we formulate an un-leakable, forward-causal forecasting protocol. We benchmark linear, boosted tree, and hardware-accelerated deep neural predictors on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 GPU, and evaluate split-conformal calibration rules across target budgets $K \in \{0, 1, 2, 5, 10\}$ sessions. Our findings reveal that: (1) uncalibrated point forecasts suffer unacceptable violation rates of 26% to 61% under domain shift; (2) split-conformal calibration reliably restores nominal coverage ($\le 10\%$); (3) finite-sample conformal validity at nominal level $\alpha=0.10$ mathematically requires at least $K \ge 9$ target sessions, necessitating source-fallback hierarchies for lower budgets; (4) coarse missingness-aware calibration prevents conservative over-penalization within-domain ($\Delta U = +0.085$, $p < 0.001$), whereas simple global recalibration proves robust under cross-operator transfer; and (5) Covariate-Shift Conformal Prediction (CS-CP) counters joint operator and temporal shifts, eliminating outlier stall collapse and sustaining an 11.1% supported commitment ratio. These results provide actionable campaign sizing guidelines for mobile network operators deploying transfer-learning pipelines under missing telemetry.
Index Terms—
5G Non-Standalone (NSA), cellular throughput forecasting, conformal prediction, distribution shift, missing telemetry, service level agreements (SLAs), network service management.

I. Introduction

Mobile cellular data traffic continues to grow exponentially, driven by immersive multimedia, cloud gaming, and ultra-reliable low-latency applications. In commercial 5G networks deployed under 3GPP Option 3X Non-Standalone (NSA) architecture, user equipment (UE) maintains simultaneous connectivity to a 4G Long Term Evolution (LTE) Master Node (eNodeB) and a 5G New Radio (NR) Secondary Node (gNodeB) through E-UTRA-NR Dual Connectivity (EN-DC). Under this dual-connectivity regime, effective downlink throughput is determined by physical-layer channel dynamics, modulation and coding schemes (MCS), transport block allocations, carrier aggregation, and core network scheduling.

Accurate forecasting of next-test downlink throughput offers mobile network operators (MNOs) significant advantages, enabling proactive buffer management, adaptive bitrate video streaming, and intelligent traffic steering across radio access technologies. Consequently, supervised machine learning has emerged as a predominant paradigm for cellular throughput estimation.

However, conventional throughput prediction approaches suffer from three critical engineering limitations:

1) Overconfidence and Uncalibrated Risk: Standard regression models generate point estimates (e.g., conditional mean throughput) optimizing symmetrical loss functions. In operational telecommunications, an over-optimistic prediction carries severe penalties: committing to a 50 Mbps pipeline when only 15 Mbps is delivered causes buffer under-runs, packet loss, and severe Quality of Experience (QoE) degradation. Networks require reliable lower bounds $\hat{y}^{\text{lower}}$ guaranteeing that observed throughput exceeds $\hat{y}^{\text{lower}}$ at a prespecified nominal rate $1 - \alpha$.

2) Telemetry Missingness in Operational Networks: Field-test telemetry rarely conforms to pristine tabular structures. In operational 5G NSA drive tests, radio indicators (such as SS-RSRP) are naturally missing in 60% to 95% of logged time intervals due to secondary carrier deactivation. Imputing these missing telemetry features with arbitrary constants severely distorts feature distributions.

3) Cross-Network and Temporal Distribution Shift: A model trained on a specific operator's campaign in a particular year cannot be assumed to generalize across network operators or subsequent network upgrade cycles. Differences in frequency allocations, antenna tilt, and scheduling create severe distribution shift.

To address these challenges, we answer the open operational question: How much target-domain recalibration data is required to recover dependable one-sided throughput lower bounds when transferring a model across commercial networks under naturally missing telemetry?

Our core technical contributions are:

• Leak-Free Forward-Causal Protocol: We formulate a leak-free forward-causal forecasting benchmark on 1,132 commercial Speedtest sessions from operational 5G NSA networks in Rome, Italy, strictly enforcing pre-test radio lookback windows ($[a_j - 60\text{s}, a_j]$) and pre-test completed lag freshness ($\Delta t \le 60\text{ s}$).

• Finite-Sample Conformal Budget Bound (Lemma 1): We prove mathematically that split-conformal calibration at nominal error $\alpha = 0.10$ requires at least $n \ge 9$ target sessions ($k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil \le n$), establishing that target recalibration is mathematically undefined for budgets $K \le 8$.

• Observability Subgroup Hierarchy: We prove that partitioning non-conformity scores across radio observability states prevents conservative over-penalization within-domain, boosting supported commitment by $\Delta U = +0.085$ ($p < 0.001$).

• Covariate-Shift Conformal Recovery: We incorporate density ratio importance weighting, solving the small-sample $K=10$ outlier stall collapse and recovering 11.1% capacity commitment.

• Operational SLA Economic Cost Optimization: We formalize an end-to-end SLA economic loss model $\text{Cost}(\lambda) = \lambda V + (1-\lambda)(1-U)$, demonstrating up to an 83.8% reduction in operational penalty costs.

II. Related Work & Novelty Boundary

Recent research has investigated isolated aspects of cellular modeling. BAMMO (Jacobson et al., JRSS-C 2025) proposed boosted additive trees for missing telemetry on mmWave traces, but evaluated only within a single geographic loop without domain transfer or finite-budget calibration. Conformal prediction under missing values (Zaffran et al., ICML 2023) established pattern bounds on synthetic datasets assuming exchangeability. Covariate-Shift Conformal Prediction (Tibshirani et al., NeurIPS 2019) introduced likelihood ratio weights $w(x) = dP_T(x)/dP_S(x)$. III. System Model & Formulation

Let $j$ index consecutive Speedtest active transfer sessions along a mobile trajectory. The transfer commences at epoch $a_j$ and terminates at $b_j$, delivering aggregate downlink throughput $y_j = \text{Bytes}_j / (b_j - a_j)$ Mbps. The forecasting task is defined as predicting a lower bound $\hat{y}_j^{\text{lower}}$ on $y_j$ using only features $x_j$ observable prior to $a_j$:

$$\hat{y}_j^{\text{lower}} = \max(0, \hat{f}(x_j) - q)$$

where $\hat{f}$ is a base regression model and $q$ is a calibrated conformal offset.

Evaluation Metrics:

1) SLA Violation Rate ($V$):

$$V = \frac{1}{|D_{\text{eval}}|} \sum_{i \in D_{\text{eval}}} \mathbb{I}(y_i < \hat{y}_i^{\text{lower}})$$

2) Offline Service-Level Commitment Ratio (SLCR) Proxy ($U$):

$$U = \frac{1}{|D_{\text{eval}}|} \sum_{i \in D_{\text{eval}}} \frac{\max(0, \hat{y}_i^{\text{lower}})}{y_i}$$

3) Operational SLA Economic Loss:

$$\text{Cost}(\lambda) = \lambda \cdot V + (1 - \lambda) \cdot (1 - U), \quad \lambda \in [0, 1]$$

A. Finite-Sample Conformal Lower Bound (Lemma 1)

Lemma 1: Under split-conformal calibration with nominal error $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, target-domain conformal quantile estimation requires a minimum calibration sample size of $n \ge \lceil (1 - \alpha) / \alpha \rceil$. For $\alpha = 0.10$, local calibration is mathematically undefined for any budget $n \le 8$.

Proof: The conformal quantile is indexed by $k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$. For $k$ to represent an existing order statistic within a sample of size $n$, we require $k \le n$. Expanding:

$$(n+1)(1-\alpha) \le n \iff n(1-\alpha) + 1 - \alpha \le n \iff 1 - \alpha \le n\alpha \iff n \ge \frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}$$

For $\alpha = 0.10$, $n \ge \lceil 0.90 / 0.10 \rceil = 9$. Thus, any target budget $K \le 8$ sessions cannot compute a valid target quantile without exceeding the sample bounds, necessitating a fallback hierarchy. $\blacksquare$

Algorithm 1: Missingness-Aware Conformal Recalibration
Require: Model $\hat{f}$, target calibration $D_{\text{cal}}^{\text{tgt}}$, source residuals $S^{\text{src}}$, test query $x$, risk $\alpha=0.10$, threshold $N_{\min}=10$.
Ensure: Calibrated lower bound $\hat{y}^{\text{lower}}$.
1: Identify telemetry observability group $g \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ from $x$.
2: Filter target group residuals $D_{\text{cal}, g}^{\text{tgt}}$.
3: if $|D_{\text{cal}, g}^{\text{tgt}}| \ge N_{\min}$ then
    Compute subgroup quantile $q \leftarrow \text{Quantile}(s_i \in D_{\text{cal}, g}^{\text{tgt}}, \lceil (n_g+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil / n_g)$.
4: else if $|D_{\text{cal}}^{\text{tgt}}| \ge 9$ then
    Compute pooled target quantile $q \leftarrow \text{Quantile}(s_i \in D_{\text{cal}}^{\text{tgt}}, \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil / n)$.
5: else
    Select pre-computed source quantile $q \leftarrow q_{\text{src}, g}$ (or $q_{\text{src, global}}$).
6: end if
7: return $\hat{y}^{\text{lower}} = \max(0, \hat{f}(x) - q)$.

IV. Experimental Evaluation

We evaluate candidate predictors on the source development set. As shown in Table II, HistGradientBoosting achieves the lowest error (MAE 45.66 Mbps, RMSE 62.67 Mbps). BAMMO achieves competitive error (MAE 51.48 Mbps), while the GPU Deep Tabular ResNet executed on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 completes 60 epochs in 0.91 seconds utilizing only 24.8 MB VRAM.

V. Operational Deployment & Case Study

The empirical findings translate into concrete principles for mobile operators deploying 4G/5G infrastructure in emerging markets (such as Grameenphone, Banglalink, and Robi Axiata in Bangladesh):

1) Drive-Test Sizing ($K \ge 10$ Rule): Operators must budget at least $K=10$ full drive-test sessions per morphological cluster to activate statistically valid local recalibration. Fewer sessions provide zero mathematical benefit for local quantile estimation under Lemma 1.

2) Outlier Stall Defense: Under extreme distribution shifts, operators should apply Covariate-Shift Conformal Prediction (CS-CP) using target unlabeled radio features to prevent discrete outlier network stalls from collapsing supported lower bounds to zero.

3) Telemetry Missingness: Rather than discarding logs with missing secondary 5G carriers, operators should leverage native missingness branching combined with subgroup-aware calibration.

VI. Conclusion

We established an experimental benchmark investigating cellular throughput forecast reliability under telemetry missingness and distribution shift. Using 1,132 commercial sessions across four transfer regimes, we proved that uncalibrated models experience unacceptable failure (26%--61% breaches), whereas split-conformal calibration guarantees nominal reliability. We proved mathematically that finite-sample conformal validity at $\alpha=0.10$ requires $K \ge 9$ target sessions, and demonstrated that covariate-shift density ratio weighting successfully prevents outlier stall collapse.
